newsitem.title: USA: Investors to see broad-based capital gains tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Investors to see broad-based capital gains tax cut.

text.p: A tax cut on profits from selling investments is virtually assured this year, and analysts predicted Monday investors will see at least seven percentage points shaved off the maximum 28 percent rate.
Congressional tax-writing committees will have $135 billion in gross tax cuts over five years to play with when they start writing legislation after Congress approves a budget blueprint.

A capital gains tax cut will compete for a share of that pie against a tax credit for families with children, estate tax relief and expansion of eligibility for Individual Retirement Accounts. Also, President Clinton was promised $35 billion for tax credits for higher education.

"The bottom line is this is probably the best chance in history to get a deep-seated capital gains tax cut," said Mark Bloomfield, president of the American Council for Capital Formation, which has pushed for such a rate reduction.
Analysts expect the top capital gains tax rate of 28 percent will end up anywhere from the 19.8 percent that Senate Republicans proposed early this year to 21 percent.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said in Chicago Monday there would be room to cut the top rate to under 20 percent.
"You would have to allow room for tax credits and other components, but I think there is enough there to get it down into that range of under 20 percent," the Mississippi Republican said.
Some groups have expressed concern that revenues lost with a lower capital gains tax rate will balloon dramatically in later years.

When tax rates on capital gains are first cut, the change acts as a revenue raiser for the government, because investors who had been holding off on selling assets rush to do so. The tax rate cut starts to lose money for the government when investors settle down.

A congressional Joint Committee on Taxation analysis of a Senate Republican capital gains tax cut proposal found it would bring $12.8 billion in revenues in fiscal 1998 but would lose revenue steadily for the next nine years. The shortfall would be $20.1 billion in fiscal 2007.

"The costs in the short-run are artificially small because when you cut the rate, you get a sudden increase in realisation (of gains)," said Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. He called it the "unlocking effect."
The budget framework calls for net tax cuts of $85 billion in the first five years, $165 billion in the second five years for a total of $250 billion net tax cuts over 10 years.

"I think the tax package is the most troubling part of the budget agreement," said Robert Greenstein, executive director of the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorites. "In the second five years, tax cuts are twice as big as in the first five years," he said.

The early Senate Republican bill had given an effective date for a capital gains tax cut of Jan. 1, 1997. The effective date can affect the behaviour of investors. If it is set in the future, they may hold off on selling assets until then. Congress does not want to affect market behaviour, analysts said.

The effective date was likely to be the date the legislation passed the tax writing committees, some analysts said. Reischauer said he believed the effective date would be May 2, the date of the announced budget deal.

Another issue the tax-writing committees will have to decide is whether to allow taking into account the effects of inflation on an asset. Such "indexing" would be more costly to the government because investors would pay tax on a smaller gain calculation.
